stories.headline: Colorado's largest lumber mill closing, threatening 400 jobs and $75 million in local payroll
stories.summary:
Montrose Forest Products, Colorado's largest lumber mill, is shutting down after owner Neiman Enterprises failed to find a buyer willing to continue operations. The company informed its 90 direct employees Tuesday that work would wind down once the remaining timber supply runs out in the coming weeks. If no viable offer emerges within 60 days, the mill will sell its equipment.

The closure could cost more than 400 direct and indirect workers their livelihoods and remove nearly $75 million in annual payroll spending from the Montrose economy, according to the Montrose Economic Development Corp. Local officials describe the loss as the largest economic blow to the city of 21,000 since Russell Stover Chocolates shuttered its factory in 2020.

The mill was one of only three commercial-scale lumber operations remaining in Colorado, a state that has seen its mill count fall from 87 to 33 since 1987. Industry leaders warn the closure will have a ripple effect on the broader Colorado timber sector and could make large-scale forest restoration efforts significantly more expensive.

Rising fuel costs, uncertain timber supplies from nearby national forests, and a roughly 30% increase in operating costs since the pandemic pushed the mill past viability. Without a functioning timber market, officials say diseased and overcrowded forests could elevate wildfire risk and threaten watersheds, including one that supplies Grand Junction.

stories.headline: United Airlines cancels 9/11 flyover over Denver after community concerns
stories.summary:
United Airlines canceled a planned flyover of a passenger jet escorted by F-16s over Denver on the eve of the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, citing 'concerns in the community.' The flight was to depart Denver International Airport at 8:15 a.m. Thursday, with the Boeing 777 joined by jets from the 120th Fighter Squadron at Buckley Space Force Base before passing over United's flight training center in the Central Park neighborhood.

Denver's Office of Emergency Management had published a public notice earlier in the week alerting residents to expect a highly visible and audible, but brief, planned event. City officials said they understood the flyover as a tribute to victims, pilots and aviation workers, but recognized it could cause alarm.

United did not elaborate on the specific concerns that led to the cancellation. Mayor Mike Johnston's office said the decision to cancel rested with the airline, while acknowledging the public notice had successfully warned residents ahead of time.

Separate 9/11 memorial activities will continue. United and American Airlines employees will observe a moment of silence at DIA at 9:03 a.m. Friday, and United is unveiling a monument made from World Trade Center steel at its Denver training center to honor crew members from United Flight 175 and Flight 93.

stories.headline: Four protesters arraigned in Arapahoe County after July anti-ICE demonstration in Centennial
stories.summary:
Four people arrested during a July anti-ICE demonstration outside a federal field office in Centennial were arraigned Wednesday in Arapahoe County District Court, with dozens of supporters filling the courtroom and rallying outside. Yoselin Corrales, Arnie Carter, Mateo Henry and Terry Burnsed each face charges of obstructing a passageway; Corrales and Henry also face obstruction of a peace officer charges.

The charges stem from a July 20 protest at 12445 E. Caley Ave., where more than 100 people gathered to demonstrate against ICE enforcement actions and conditions at immigration detention facilities. Attorneys for the defendants characterized the charges as an attempt to suppress First Amendment activity, noting that obstruction charges are commonly used against protesters.

The arraignments come as immigration arrests in Colorado have surged. ICE detained 495 people in Colorado in July alone, a 93% increase from March, according to a Denver Post data analysis. Legal filings by Colorado attorneys allege immigration agents acted illegally and violently during several of those arrests.

The protest in July occurred days after Adams County health officials confirmed an active tuberculosis investigation at the Aurora immigration detention center. The Colorado Attorney General's Office subsequently filed a federal lawsuit alleging detention center officials ignored deadlines to turn over health records.

stories.headline: Denver school board convenes after antisemitism allegation but again avoids resolving dispute
stories.summary:
Denver Public Schools board members met Wednesday for the first time since Board President Xóchitl Gaytán accused Director Monica Hunter of making an antisemitic comment, but the session ended without a formal investigation being announced or key allegations resolved. The meeting instead devolved into procedural disputes over whether Gaytán had followed proper process in presenting policy violation allegations against Hunter and Director Donald 'D.J.' Torres.

Gaytán has not publicly identified who Hunter made the alleged comment about or specified the language she deemed antisemitic. Her email to Hunter indicated the language was used in connection with Hunter's opposition to supporting a board colleague for an officer position and her refusal to sit next to that colleague on the dais. The only new board member who did not receive an officer title is Amy Klein Molk, who is Jewish.

Directors John Youngquist and Kimberlee Sia said they want more information and a formal investigation into the antisemitism allegation, a call Hunter said she welcomed. However, the board took no formal action, marking the third time in recent months it has scheduled a meeting to address internal disputes without resolving them.

Superintendent Alex Marrero told the board the situation is 'untenable' for district staff, who are caught in the middle of the ongoing feuds. He encouraged continued dialogue but stopped short of calling for outside intervention.

stories.headline: Weld County approves what could become Colorado's largest data center near Windsor
stories.summary:
The Weld County Board of Commissioners voted 5-0 Wednesday to approve a special-use permit for a proposed 41-acre data center on the former Carestream Health site in an unincorporated area near Windsor. New York-based Global AI is developing the project, which could become the largest data center in Colorado.

During a public hearing, community members raised concerns about water consumption, noise, strain on the electrical grid, and the company's lack of outreach to nearby residents. A Global AI representative acknowledged the company had not contacted surrounding residents before the hearing, calling the omission a possible 'fault.'

Residents who spoke against the permit said they had received little advance notice and lacked sufficient information about potential health and community impacts, including the project's proximity to residential areas. Critics also pointed out that Global AI is only two years old and has no established track record in Colorado.

Despite the objections, commissioners approved the permit unanimously. Opponents said they intend to continue monitoring the project and will seek accountability as it moves forward.

stories.headline: Colorado's top public company CEO earned nearly $40 million in 2025, led by Liberty Media's new chief
stories.summary:
Derek Chang, the CEO of Formula 1 parent company Liberty Media, was Colorado's highest-compensated public company executive in 2025, receiving a package of nearly $40 million in his first year leading the firm, according to SEC filings compiled by BusinessDen. The majority of the package consisted of stock awards tied to his appointment as CEO at the start of the year, along with a $2.2 million base salary and a $1.2 million sign-on bonus.

Westminster-based tech firm Trimble ranked second, paying CEO Robert Painter $19.1 million, slightly up from the prior year. VF Corp CEO Bracken Darrell rounded out the top three at $18.9 million, nearly double his 2024 compensation while overseeing brands including The North Face, Vans and Timberland.

DaVita CEO Javier Rodriguez finished fourth and led executives in corporate jet usage, logging $460,615 in personal flight time. Palantir CEO Alex Karp, whose company relocated from Denver to Florida earlier this year, reported $2 million in chartered flights and $2.5 million in personal security costs. EchoStar CEO Charlie Ergen topped the list for air travel expenses at $3.4 million.

The annual compensation survey covers the top 25 paid executives at publicly traded companies headquartered in the Denver region, based on proxy statements filed with the SEC.

stories.headline: Denver councilman's promised tipped wage proposal still hasn't materialized, six months later
stories.summary:
Denver City Councilman Darrell Watson pledged in February to introduce a proposal addressing the city's tipped minimum wage structure within a month, but six months later no proposal has been filed. Watson declined interview requests and his spokesman offered no timeline, saying only that the office is 'listening to the community.'

Denver's current minimum wage stands at $19.29 per hour, with a $3.02 tip credit bringing the tipped minimum to $16.27. Those figures will rise to $19.84 and $16.82 in January, levels that restaurateurs say exceed rates in New York and San Francisco and are contributing to a contracting local food and beverage industry.

A city-sponsored report released alongside Watson's February pledge offered several recommendations, including creating a middle-tier wage to allow tip sharing between front-of-house and back-of-house workers, and potentially reverting to Colorado's state tipped minimum of $12.14 with anti-erosion protections. The report's authors say they have received no meaningful updates since February.

Industry advocates say momentum on the issue has stalled. Watson faces reelection next year, and observers note the issue is politically sensitive given differing constituencies within the restaurant industry. Cities including Chicago and Washington, D.C., have reversed course on similar high tipped minimum wage policies in recent years.

stories.headline: Colorado River negotiation process under scrutiny as states fail to reach post-2026 agreement
stories.summary:
As states sharing the Colorado River fail to reach a new agreement governing water use after 2026, growing criticism is being directed at the closed-door negotiation process itself, according to reporting by CPR News. Advocates and some officials are questioning how much of the negotiation should be visible to the public given the stakes for Western water users.

Colorado is one of seven states dependent on the Colorado River, which has faced chronic overallocation and severe drought conditions in recent years. Negotiations over post-2026 operating guidelines have dragged on without a final deal, raising concerns about what framework will govern the river when current agreements expire.

Critics of the process argue that the lack of transparency has allowed negotiations to stall without adequate public input, while some negotiators contend that confidential talks are necessary to reach compromise among competing state interests. The outcome will have significant implications for Colorado water users, agriculture and municipal systems that rely on the river's flow.

stories.headline: Proposed Colorado Springs AI data center would consume more power than city's largest current customer
stories.summary:
A proposed artificial intelligence data center in northwest Colorado Springs, known as Project Taurus, would consume approximately 50 megawatts of electricity continuously during its first year of operation — more than the city's current largest power customer uses, according to CPR News. The project is being considered for an existing building and would scale up power usage significantly over time.

The proposal arrives as AI-driven data centers are expanding rapidly across Colorado, raising questions about grid capacity, utility rates for other customers, and water use associated with cooling systems. Weld County approved a separate large data center project near Windsor on the same day.

Colorado Springs Utilities and city officials are evaluating the project's potential impact on the local electrical grid. The scale of the power demand has drawn attention from residents and policymakers concerned about infrastructure strain and the allocation of public utility resources to large commercial users.

stories.headline: DNA scandal's fallout will reverberate through Colorado's courts for decades, legal experts say
stories.summary:
The conviction and sentencing of former Colorado Bureau of Investigation analyst Missy Woods for deliberately altering DNA evidence in hundreds of cases has set off a legal reckoning that experts say will affect Colorado's criminal justice system for years, if not decades, according to CPR News. Attorneys and prosecutors are working through the scope of cases potentially tainted by her misconduct.

Woods' manipulations affected hundreds of criminal cases, meaning convictions could be challenged, retrials ordered, and settlements reached across multiple jurisdictions. Defense attorneys are reviewing case files to identify clients who may have been wrongly convicted or whose outcomes were influenced by fraudulent lab results.

The scandal has also prompted broader scrutiny of oversight practices at crime laboratories in Colorado, with calls for reforms to audit processes and whistleblower protections. Officials are still working to determine the full universe of affected cases, a process that legal experts say could take years to complete.

stories.headline: Sean Payton hands play-calling duties to offensive coordinator Davis Webb ahead of season opener
stories.summary:
Denver Broncos head coach Sean Payton announced he will no longer call offensive plays in 2026, handing those responsibilities to new offensive coordinator Davis Webb. The move represents a significant shift in how the offense will be run under Payton, who has traditionally maintained a hands-on role in game-day play calling.

Webb drew interest from other NFL teams as an offensive coordinator candidate this offseason before the Broncos retained him and expanded his role. Payton's decision to step back from play-calling could be aimed at allowing him to manage the full game more effectively as Denver pursues a Super Bowl run.

The announcement comes just ahead of Denver's Week 1 Monday Night Football game at Kansas City, with the Broncos entering the season with high expectations and a largely intact roster. Nine team captains, voted on by players, were also named this week.

stories.headline: Broncos teammates identify defensive tackle Eni Uwazurike as top breakout candidate for 2026
stories.summary:
Denver Broncos players and coaches have singled out defensive tackle Eni Uwazurike as the player most likely to break out during the 2026 season, according to a Denver Post survey conducted during training camp. Uwazurike, a fourth-round pick in 2022, missed the 2023 season due to a gambling suspension and played a limited role in 2024 before emerging as a consistent disruptive force this preseason.

With veteran defensive tackle John Franklin-Myers departing for the Tennessee Titans in free agency, Uwazurike is expected to assume a much larger role alongside All-Pro Zach Allen. Fellow defensive tackle D.J. Jones called Uwazurike 'unblockable,' and coach Sean Payton noted he has played 'really well' throughout camp.

Uwazurike finished the 2025 season with 39 tackles, five tackles for loss and five quarterback hits, primarily as a run-stopper. He has worked to expand his pass-rushing skills this offseason and has shown improved quickness for a 320-pound lineman, according to teammates. Wide receiver Pat Bryant and other players cited him as a player opponents will have trouble containing.

topStory.headline: Rhode Island Gov. McKee Defeated in Democratic Primary, First Governor to Lose Primary Since 2018
topStory.summary:
Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee lost his Democratic primary Tuesday to Helena Foulkes, a former CVS Health executive, becoming the first sitting governor to fall in a primary election since 2018. Public polling had shown McKee trailing Foulkes by double digits heading into the vote, and Foulkes outspent him on television advertising by a margin of 3-to-1, according to ad-tracking firm AdImpact.

McKee, 75, has served as governor since 2021, when he assumed the office after Gov. Gina Raimondo was appointed by President Joe Biden to serve as Secretary of Commerce. His tenure was heavily defined by the December 2023 closure of the Washington Bridge, a major commuter thoroughfare in Providence, after state engineers discovered broken anchor rods and significant structural problems. An Emerson College poll conducted in August found that 63 percent of likely Rhode Island voters disapproved of McKee's handling of the bridge closure, with just 18 percent expressing approval. McKee defended the closure as a safety-driven decision and has said the reconstruction, now projected to cost $427 million and running behind its original schedule, will be completed by 2028.

Foulkes, 62, has no prior elected office experience but carries significant political connections. Her uncle and grandfather, Chris Dodd and Thomas Dodd, both served as U.S. senators from Connecticut, and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi — a college roommate of Foulkes' mother — campaigned on her behalf. Foulkes ran on issues of housing affordability and economic growth, including a proposed Millionaire's Tax that would impose an additional 3 percent levy on incomes exceeding $1 million to fund construction of more than 20,000 new homes. Political scientists who spoke with CBS News characterized the race less as a contest of competing policy platforms and more as a referendum on McKee's performance in office.

The last Democratic governor to lose a primary was Hawaii's Neil Abercrombie in 2014, who fell to state Sen. David Ige by 35 percentage points. On the Republican side, Kansas Gov. Jeff Colyer lost his 2018 primary to then-Secretary of State Kris Kobach. McKee's defeat comes amid a broader wave of anti-incumbent sentiment that has already claimed eleven House members and two U.S. senators in primaries this election cycle. Foulkes enters the general election as a heavy favorite in a state that has not elected a Republican governor since 2010 and that Vice President Kamala Harris carried by nearly 14 points in the 2024 presidential election.
